query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In a dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy protective coating, the presence of an interconnected, harder BCC phase and its coherent interfaces with the FCC matrix act as barriers to dislocation motion. This microstructural feature elevates the activation energy required for creep deformation under sustained loading, thereby enhancing creep resistance compared to a single-phase FCC coating.
generation.material_initial_state: A protective coating exhibiting a dual-phase microstructure with a roughly interpenetrating FCC matrix and BCC phase (or B2‐like phase) distributed as a continuous network or lamellae.
generation.intervention: Apply a constant sustained stress (below the yield limit) at an elevated temperature within the operational boundary to both the dual-phase coating and a controlled, comparable single-phase FCC protective coating.
generation.conditions: Continuous loading at a constant stress (e.g., ~70-80% of yield strength) and elevated temperatures where creep mechanisms are prominent, but below any phase transformation threshold that would induce additional microstructural changes.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherent or semi-coherent interfaces between the FCC and BCC phases that pin dislocation movement and slow the progression of plastic deformation.
generation.mechanism: Under applied stress, dislocations in the FCC phase are hindered at the FCC/BCC interfaces, delaying dislocation nucleation and motion. The BCC phase, with its higher lattice friction and inherent resistance to dislocation glide, acts as an anchoring network, effectively reducing the overall creep strain rate by requiring higher energy for dislocation bypass.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the single-phase FCC baseline, the dual-phase FCC/BCC coating should exhibit a significantly lower creep strain rate and reduced progressive plastic deformation. Microstructural analysis post-creep testing would reveal that dislocation activity is concentrated near the phase boundaries, with less overall macroscopic deformation in the dual-phase system.
generation.baseline: A homogeneous FCC high-entropy alloy coating subjected to an identical sustained stress and temperature regime.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected to operate within the stress range below the yield limit and at temperatures where creep is thermally activated yet below levels that compromise phase stability.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the creep rate reduction and the sensitivity of the mechanism to variations in phase morphology, volume fraction, and interface coherence require further quantitative investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of otherwise compositionally identical high-entropy alloy coatings: one with a dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructure achieved via controlled solidification (e.g., using a eutectic alloy design) and a second with a single-phase FCC microstructure obtained through processing modifications. Subject both sets to identical constant-load creep tests at an elevated temperature and stress level (within the operational boundary). Use high-resolution microscopy (TEM/EBSD) to monitor dislocation activity, interface behavior, and overall creep strain over time.
measurements: Creep strain rate as a function of time
Dislocation density and distribution (with special attention to phase boundaries)
Microstructural characterization of phase integrity and interface morphology before and after creep testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dual-phase FCC/BCC coating does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in creep strain rate (or shows similar or higher creep deformation) compared to the single-phase FCC baseline under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that interface-mediated barrier effects from the BCC phase are responsible for enhanced creep resistance must be rejected.

Creep Behavior and Its Influencing Factors in High-Entropy Superalloys: A Molecular Dynamics Simulation Study

Abstract: AbstractIn aero-engine applications, turbine blades operate under high-temperature and high-pressure thermomechanical cyclic loading conditions, which demand exceptional mechanical performance. High-entropy superalloys, characterized by a stable dual-phase γ/γ′ microstructure, have emerged as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials due to their superior creep resistance. In this study, the creep behaviors of high-entropy superalloys are systematically investigated using molecular dynamics simulations, exploring the effects of stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction on creep deformation mechanisms. The results show that both stress and temperature significantly influence creep behavior, with temperature exerting a more dominant effect. As the applied stress increases, the dominant creep mechanism evolves from atomic diffusion to dislocation nucleation and motion, eventually leading to phase transformation. A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.
